{{Short description|Statistical measure of fit}}

In statistics, '''pseudo-R-squared''' values are used when the outcome variable is nominal or ordinal such that the [[coefficient of determination]] {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> cannot be applied as a measure for [[goodness of fit]] and when a [[likelihood function]] is used to fit a model.

In [[linear regression]], the squared multiple correlation, {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> is used to assess goodness of fit as it represents the proportion of variance in the criterion that is explained by the predictors.<ref name=Cohen>{{cite book | last1 = Cohen  | first1 = Jacob
  | first2= Patricia |last2=Cohen |first3= Steven G. |last3= West |first4= Leona S. |last4= Aiken | author4-link= Leona S. Aiken
  | title = Applied Multiple Regression/Correlation Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences |edition= 3rd
  | publisher = Routledge
  | year = 2002 | pages = 502 | isbn = 978-0-8058-2223-6 }} 
</ref> 
In [[logistic regression]] analysis, there is no agreed upon analogous measure, but there are several competing measures each with limitations.<ref name=Cohen/><ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=https://support.sas.com/resources/papers/proceedings14/1485-2014.pdf |title=Measures of fit for logistic regression |last=Allison |first=Paul D. |publisher=Statistical Horizons LLC and the University of Pennsylvania}}</ref>

Some commonly used indices are examined in this article:
* Likelihood ratio {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|L}}
* Unadjusted and adjusted geometric mean squared improvement {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|M}} and {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|N}}
* Tjur {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|T}}

== {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|L}} by McFadden==
The pseudo {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> credited to McFadden (sometimes called '''[[likelihood ratio]] index'''<ref>Hardin, J. W., Hilbe, J. M. (2007). Generalized linear models and extensions. USA: Taylor & Francis. Page 60, [https://books.google.com/books?id=tOeqO6Hs-6gC&dq=%22likelihood%20ratio%20index%22%20pseudo%20r2&pg=PA60 Google Books]</ref> or '''log-likelihood ratio {{mvar|R<sup>2</sup>}}'''<ref name = "menard"/>) is defined as<ref>{{cite journal | title = Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behaviour | first = Daniel | last = McFadden | date = 1972 | page = 23 | journal = Working Paper Np. 199/BART 10}}</ref>

::<math>R^2_\text{L} = 1 - \frac{\ln(L_M)}{\ln(L_0)}, </math>

or expressed using [[deviance (statistics)|deviance]]<ref name=Cohen/> rather than likelihood

::<math>R^2_\text{L} = \frac{D_\text{0} - D_\text{M}} {D_\text{0}}</math>

and is preferred over {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|M}} by [[Paul D. Allison]].<ref name=":0"/> The two expressions {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|L}} and {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|M}} are then related respectively by,

::<math> \begin{matrix} R^2_\text{M} = 1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{L_0}\right)^{\frac{2(R^2_\text{L})}{n}} \\ [1.5em] R^2_\text{L} = -\dfrac{n}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\ln( 1 - R^2_\text{M} )}{\ln L_0} \end{matrix}</math>

This is the most analogous index to the squared multiple correlations in linear regression.<ref name=Menard>{{cite book | last = Menard
  | first = Scott W.
  | title = Applied Logistic Regression |edition= 2nd
  | publisher = SAGE
  | year = 2002 | isbn = 978-0-7619-2208-7 }} {{page needed | date=May 2012}}</ref> It represents the proportional reduction in the [[deviance (statistics)|deviance]] wherein the deviance is treated as a measure of variation analogous but not identical to the [[variance]] in [[linear regression]] analysis.<ref name=Menard/> One limitation of the likelihood ratio {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> is that it is not monotonically related to the odds ratio,<ref name=Cohen/> meaning that it does not necessarily increase as the odds ratio increases and does not necessarily decrease as the odds ratio decreases.

=== Adjusted ===

The adjusted version includes the number of predictors {{mvar|K}} as a penalisation term<ref>{{cite web | access-date = 2026-03-25 | title = FAQ: What are pseudo R-squareds? | publisher = [[UCLA]] | url = https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-what-are-pseudo-r-squareds/}}</ref>

::<math>R^2_\text{L} = 1 - \frac{\ln(L_M) - K}{\ln(L_0)}, </math>

== {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup><sub>M</sub> by Cox and Snell ==
{{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup><sub>M</sub> is an alternative index of goodness of fit described by Maddala in 1983 attributed to Cox and Snell<ref name = "menard"/> related to the {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> value from linear regression (sometimes called '''geometric mean squared improvement per observation {{mvar|R<sup>2</sup>}}'''<ref name = "menard"/>).<ref name=":0"/> It is given by:

::<math>
\begin{align}
R^2_\text{M} & = 1 - \left(\frac{L_0}{L_M}\right)^{2/n} \\[5pt]
& = 1 - \exp \left(\frac{2}{n}(\ln(L_0) - \ln(L_M)) \right)
\end{align}
</math>

where {{mvar|L{{sub|M}}}} and {{mvar|L{{sub|0}}}} are the likelihoods for the model being fitted and the null model, respectively, {{mvar|\ln}} denotes the [[natural logarithm]], and {{mvar|n}} is the number of observations. {{mvar|L{{sub|0}}}} is the model with just an intercept.<ref name = "menard">{{cite journal | first = Scott | last = Menard | title = Coefficients of Determination for Multiple Logistic Regression | journal = American Statistician | doi = 10.2307/2685605 | volume = 54 | date = 2000 | number = 1 | pages = 17-24}}</ref> The Cox and [[Joyce Snell|Snell]] index corresponds to the standard {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> in case of a linear model with normal error. In certain situations, {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup><sub>M</sub> may be problematic as its maximum value is <math>1 - L_0^{2/n}</math> which means it never takes the value of one. For example, for logistic regression, the upper bound is <math>R^2_\text{M}\leq0.75</math> for a symmetric [[marginal distribution]] of events and decreases further for an asymmetric distribution of events.<ref name=":0" />

=== Adjusted {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup><sub>M</sub> by Nagelkerke ===

[[Nico Nagelkerke]] in a highly cited [[Biometrika]] paper,<ref>Nagelkerke, N. J. D. (1991). A Note on a General Definition of the Coefficient of Determination. ''Biometrika'', 78(3), 691–692. https://doi.org/10.2307/2337038</ref> provides a correction to the Cox and Snell {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> so that the maximum value is equal to 1. This correction is done by dividing {{mvar|R}}<sub>M</sub> by its upper bound.<ref name=":0"/><ref name = "menard"/>

::<math>
\begin{align}
R^2_\text{N} & = \frac{\left[1 - \left(\frac{L_0}{L_M}\right)^{2/n}\right]}{1 - L_0^{2/n}}
\end{align}
</math>

Nevertheless, the Cox and Snell and likelihood ratio {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>s show greater agreement with each other than either does with the adjusted Nagelkerke {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>.<ref name=Cohen/> Of course, this might not be the case for values exceeding 0.75 as the Cox and Snell index is capped at this value{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}. The likelihood ratio {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> is often preferred{{citation needed|reason = Preferred by who?|date=March 2026}} to the alternatives as it is most analogous to {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> in [[linear regression]], is independent of the base rate (both Cox and Snell and Nagelkerke {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>s increase as the proportion of cases increase from 0 to 0.5) and varies between 0 and 1.

== {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|T}} by Tjur==

Tjur proposed an alternative measure of {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup>{{sub|T}},<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tjur |first=Tue |year=2009 |title=Coefficients of determination in logistic regression models |journal=American Statistician |volume=63 |issue=4 |pages=366–372 |doi=10.1198/tast.2009.08210 |s2cid=121927418 }}</ref> which is in two steps:
# For each level of the dependent variable, find the mean of the predicted probabilities of an event.
# Take the absolute value of the difference between these means

This quantity is not an <math>R^2</math> per se, however Tjur shows how it is related to usual <math>R^2</math> metrics.

== Example ==

This displays [[R (programming language)|R]] output from calculating pseudo-r-squared values using the "pscl" package by Simon Jackman. The pseudo-R-squared calculated using the formule named for McFadden is labelled “McFadden”. Next to this, the pseudo-r-squared by Cox and Snell is labelled “r2ML” and this type of pseudo-R-squared By Cox and Snell is sometimes simply called “ML”. The last value listed, labelled “r2CU” is the pseudo-r-squared by Nagelkerke and is the same as the pseudo-r-squared by Cragg and Uhler.

[[File:Pseudo-R-Squared Outputted Values from R.png|640x640px]]

== Interpretation ==

A word of caution is in order when interpreting pseudo-{{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> statistics. The reason these indices of fit are referred to as ''pseudo'' {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> is that they do not represent the proportionate reduction in error as the {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> in [[linear regression]] does.<ref name=Cohen/> Linear regression assumes [[homoscedasticity]], that the error variance is the same for all values of the criterion. Logistic regression will always be [[heteroscedastic]] – the error variances differ for each value of the predicted score. For each value of the predicted score there would be a different value of the proportionate reduction in error. Therefore, it is inappropriate to think of {{mvar|R}}<sup>2</sup> as a proportionate reduction in error in a universal sense in logistic regression.<ref name=Cohen/>
